title: deterministic-throughput-contracts-and-policy-driven-cross-zone-evacuation
creator: Lin Zhao
description: Goal: Build deterministic throughput contracts and a policy-driven cross-zone evacuation mechanism for regional dedicated fleets that preserve data residency guarantees and provide predictable SLA behavior during capacity events. This initiative covers new config primitives, autoscaler policy extensions, placement decision logic, a staged evacuation corridor, and console/CLI controls for operators and tenant admins. The feature should make it possible for customers to purchase explicit throughput SLOs for a region, specify residency constraints, and choose how we handle zone-level failures (immediate failover, delayed corridor, or degraded best-effort), all while keeping cost signals and observability surfaced in the Console.
acceptance_criteria: API: Create/update dedicated pool with throughput_contract (tokens_per_sec) and residency_scope (region|zone|none) returns 200 and persists in config
Autoscaler: Supports new policy types: 'steady-reserve', 'predictive-headroom', and 'safety-fallback' with documented behavior

Placement: Placement engine can compute deterministic allocation that honors residency_scope and a 'placement_preference' enum (zone_strict, zone_preferred, spread, cost_opt) and exposes chosen strategy in telemetry
Failover: On single-zone outage, system triggers 'evacuation corridor' that routes up to X% of traffic to alternate zones for up to Y minutes before full failover; configurable per-pool
Data residency: Requests originating with residency_lock set must not be served outside pinned region; attempts are rejected unless pool-level policy allows temporary spillover with audit log
Observability: Console shows pool-level throughput commitment, current burn-rate, headroom, and a timeline view when evacuation corridor is active
Backward compatibility: Existing pools without new fields default to previous autoscaler behavior (reactive, no deterministic throughput guarantees)
E2E tests: Simulated zone outage reproduces corridor behavior and metrics in CI; no customer request served outside residency when residency_lock=true
design_notes: We will implement throughput contracts as a soft reservation backed by a combination of reserved vCPU/GPU fractions and prioritization tokens in the scheduler. The autoscaler will expose three policy families: reactive (current), reserved-steady (keeps a steady capacity aligned to contract), and adaptive-predictive (ML-driven lookahead using recent traffic histograms). Placement decisions extend the existing allocator with a two-step scoring function: first filter by residency rules, then score by placement_preference and available headroom. 'Evacuation corridor' is a staged policy: initially route a configurable fraction to fallback zones using priority lanes and degraded QoS, then after a grace-window either failover entirely or escalate to emergency capacity pool. All policy actions emit structured audit events with reason, operator, and TTL. Configuration stored in pool metadata with an immutable contract_id for billing reconciliation.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (canary): Implement config schema, API, and unit tests; enable feature flag for internal test accounts in us-west1 and eu-west1. Phase 2 (pilot): Open to two enterprise customers; run simulated zone outage drills and collect metrics. Phase 3: Gradual opt-in for new dedicated pools; migrate existing enterprise pools only after sign-off. Phase 4: GA with Console controls and billing integration. We will provide clear migration docs and a CLI audit tool for customers to validate residency constraints before migrating.
test_plan: Unit tests for new autoscaler policies and placement filter/scorer
Integration tests for API persistence, audit events, and billing contract linkage
Chaos tests: Simulate AZ network partition and verify corridor behavior and eventual failover
E2E residency tests: Verify residency_lock prevents cross-region serving; simulate emergency-spill override with explicit operator approval
Performance bench: Verify steady-reserve policy maintains target throughput under baseline load without large latency regressions
